readings.title: Proem
readings.challenge: Follow a pattern that leaps across thousands of years in each stanza.
readings.focus: A speaker who claims the whole history of Black people, its labour, its music and its suffering, as his own.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. A proem is an introduction; this poem opens the book. Caesar ruled ancient Rome; the Woolworth Building in New York was the world’s tallest when finished in 1913; sorrow songs are spirituals; ragtime was an early form of jazz piano. In the Congo Free State, ruled by the Belgian king around 1900, workers’ hands were cut off as punishment.
readings.contentNote: The poem uses “Negro,” the respectful term of its time, as a proud self-description. It refers to slavery, the mutilation of Congolese workers under Belgian rule, and lynching.

excerpt.locator: “Proem,” the opening poem of the book; opens “I am a Negro: Black as the night is black, Black like the depths of my Africa.”; closes “I am a Negro: Black as the night is black, Black like the depths of my Africa.”.

questions.prompt: In each middle stanza, the speaker jumps from a distant past to the recent present. Trace the jump in two stanzas.
facilitatorNotes: Caesar’s door-steps lead to George Washington’s boots; the pyramids to the Woolworth Building; Africa to Georgia and spirituals to ragtime; the Congo to Texas. Each stanza joins the ancient world to the speaker’s own America, so the history never feels finished.
evidence:
Under my hand the pyramids arose.
I made mortar for the Woolworth Building.

questions.prompt: Two roles name what was done to the speaker and two name what he made. Why include both?
facilitatorNotes: As slave and victim he suffers; as worker and singer he builds pyramids and skyscrapers and creates music the whole country loves. Putting them side by side refuses to let the history be only suffering or only triumph. Readers can discuss which line hits hardest and why “now” in the lynching line matters.
evidence: I made ragtime.
They lynch me now in Texas.

questions.prompt: The first stanza returns as the last. How has its meaning changed after the middle of the poem?
facilitatorNotes: At first it is a plain statement of identity; after the list of labour, art and suffering it sounds like a proud claim to all of that history. “My Africa” claims a homeland the speaker may never have seen. Some readers hear defiance, others sorrow; both are supported by the repeated, steady lines.
evidence:
Black as the night is black,
Black like the depths of my Africa.

readings.title: Jazzonia
readings.challenge: Hear how small changes in repeated lines shift a poem’s mood.
readings.focus: A night in a Harlem nightclub turns into a question about beauty, boldness and judgment.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. Jazz was new and thrilling in 1920s Harlem; a cabaret is a nightclub with music and dancing; “jazzers” are jazz musicians. In the Bible, Eve is the first woman, blamed for the loss of the garden of Eden; Cleopatra was a famously beautiful queen of ancient Egypt. Hughes made up the title.

excerpt.locator: “Jazzonia,” the whole poem; opens “Oh, silver tree! Oh, shining rivers of the soul!”; closes “In a whirling cabaret Six long-headed jazzers play.”.

questions.prompt: The poem alternates two kinds of stanza. What are they, and what changes each time the short refrain returns?
facilitatorNotes: Cabaret stanzas show the musicians and the dancer; refrain stanzas call out to a tree and “rivers of the soul.” The adjectives shift each time: silver, singing, shining tree; shining, then silver rivers. The words swap places like dancers changing partners, so the refrain itself seems to move to the music.
evidence:
Oh, silver tree!
Oh, shining rivers of the soul!

Oh, shining tree!
Oh, silver rivers of the soul!

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker ask about Eve and Cleopatra after describing the dancing girl?
facilitatorNotes: The dancer’s eyes are “bold,” a word that could condemn her. By asking whether Eve’s eyes were “just a bit too bold,” the speaker links the dancer to the most famous women in history and questions the old habit of blaming a woman’s boldness. The poem only asks; readers can decide whether it admires the dancer or simply wonders.
evidence:
Were Eve’s eyes
In the first garden
Just a bit too bold?

questions.prompt: The last two lines repeat the second stanza with one change. What is the change, and how does it affect the ending?
facilitatorNotes: “Harlem cabaret” becomes “whirling cabaret.” The place has dissolved into motion; the poem ends in the middle of the music, without a conclusion, as if the dance goes on after we leave.
evidence:
In a whirling cabaret
Six long-headed jazzers play.

readings.title: Cross
readings.challenge: Find several meanings in a one-word title and explain how a simple ballad form carries a hard question.
readings.focus: A speaker with a white father and a Black mother forgives both and wonders where he belongs.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. In the America of the 1920s, segregation laws and customs kept white and Black people apart, and children of mixed families were often accepted by neither.
readings.contentNote: The speaker once cursed both parents and wished his mother “in hell.” The poem describes the racial inequality of the time.

excerpt.locator: “Cross,” the whole poem; opens “My old man’s a white old man And my old mother’s black. If ever I cursed my white old man…”; closes “…My ma died in a shack. I wonder where I’m gonna die, Being neither white nor black?”.

questions.prompt: In the first two stanzas, what does the speaker take back? What might have made him curse his parents in the first place?
facilitatorNotes: He takes back curses against his white father and an “evil wish” against his Black mother. Perhaps he blamed each for the position he was born into; now he wishes both well. The poem does not explain the anger, so readers can suggest reasons from the last stanza.
evidence:
If ever I cursed my white old man
I take my curses back.

questions.prompt: What does the contrast in the third stanza show about the parents’ lives?
facilitatorNotes: The father dies in a “fine big house,” the mother in a “shack”: two people joined in one family lived on opposite sides of a racial and economic line. The plain, rhyming statement makes the injustice sound like a simple fact of the world, which is part of its force.
evidence:
My old man died in a fine big house.
My ma died in a shack.

questions.prompt: The title “Cross” can mean several things. Which meanings fit the poem?
facilitatorNotes: A cross can be a mixture of two kinds, a burden to carry, a crossing point, or anger (“cross”). All fit: the speaker is of mixed parentage, carries the burden of belonging to neither side, stands where two worlds cross, and has felt rage. The final question is left unanswered.
evidence:
I wonder where I’m gonna die,
Being neither white nor black?

readings.title: Water Front Streets
readings.challenge: Work out where beauty is located in a poem that says a place is not beautiful.
readings.focus: Harbour streets that send dreamers out to sea.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. In 1923 and 1924 Hughes worked as a sailor on cargo ships to West Africa and to Europe; this poem opens the book’s section of sea poems. A water-front is the part of a town beside a harbour.

excerpt.locator: “Water Front Streets,” the poem that opens the section of the same name; opens “The spring is not so beautiful there,— But dream ships sail away To where the spring is…”; closes “…there,— But lads put out to sea Who carry beauties in their hearts And dreams, like me.”.

questions.prompt: Both stanzas begin with the same line. What place is “there,” and what does each stanza set against it?
facilitatorNotes: “There” is the water-front streets of the title. Against their plainness the first stanza sets “dream ships” sailing to a gay life; the second sets young men going to sea. The repetition admits the streets are ugly before turning to what leaves them.
evidence: The spring is not so beautiful there,—

questions.prompt: Where is beauty to be found in this poem, if not in the place itself?
facilitatorNotes: In the hearts and dreams of the young sailors, and in the distant places the ships sail toward. The lads “carry” beauty with them, so it travels instead of belonging to a spot. Readers may see hope or restless longing, or both.
evidence:
Who carry beauties in their hearts
And dreams, like me.

questions.prompt: What do the last two words, “like me,” add to the poem?
facilitatorNotes: They reveal that the speaker is one of the lads, not an onlooker. The general description becomes personal, and the poem’s longing becomes the speaker’s own. Knowing Hughes went to sea at twenty-one adds a biographical echo, though the poem works without it.
evidence: And dreams, like me.

readings.title: Death of an Old Seaman
readings.challenge: Hear how rhyme and rhythm shape the way a poem speaks about death.
readings.focus: A dead sailor’s spirit asks not to be mourned, because he has gone home to the sea.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. This poem is one of the sea poems Hughes wrote after working as a sailor in 1923 and 1924. To “strew” flowers is to scatter them.
readings.contentNote: The poem describes a burial and a voice from the dead.

excerpt.locator: “Death of an Old Seaman,” the whole poem; opens “We buried him high on a windy hill, But his soul went out to sea. I know, for I heard,…”; closes “…gone back to the wind and wave. Do not, do not weep for me, For I am happy with my sea.”.

questions.prompt: Where was the old seaman buried, and where does the speaker say his soul has gone?
facilitatorNotes: His body is “high on a windy hill,” on land, but his soul “went out to sea.” The speaker claims to have heard the soul speak “when all was still,” which sets up the second stanza as the dead man’s own words.
evidence:
We buried him high on a windy hill,
But his soul went out to sea.

questions.prompt: What three customs of mourning does the seaman refuse, and what reason does he give?
facilitatorNotes: No tombstone, no flowers, no weeping: he does not “make my bed” in the grave. The customs honour the place where the body lies, and he is not there. Readers can discuss whether the refusal comforts the living or leaves them with nothing to do.
evidence:
Put no tombstone at my head,
For here I do not make my bed.

questions.prompt: The poem is built of rhyming pairs of lines with a steady beat, like a sea song. How does the sound suit what the seaman says?
facilitatorNotes: The regular, swinging rhythm sounds like waves and like a sailors’ song, so the dead man speaks in the sea’s own music. The word “back” in “gone back” makes death a return home. The tone is calm and even happy, though some readers may hear sadness under the cheer.
evidence: I’ve gone back to the wind and wave.
For I am happy with my sea.

readings.title: Lament for Dark Peoples
readings.challenge: Identify a collective speaker and explain an extended image that judges a whole idea.
readings.focus: A voice for conquered peoples calls the modern world a “circus of civilization.”
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. A lament is a poem of mourning. Around 1900, people from Africa, Asia and the Americas were sometimes displayed to paying crowds at fairs and even in zoos.
readings.contentNote: The poem uses the period term “red man” for Native Americans and pictures Africa as jungle. It describes conquest and captivity.

excerpt.locator: “Lament for Dark Peoples,” the whole poem; opens “I was a red man one time, But the white men came. I was a black man, too, But the white…”; closes “…circus of civilization. Now I herd with the many— Caged in the circus of civilization.”.

questions.prompt: The speaker says, “I was a red man one time” and “I was a black man, too.” Who is speaking?
facilitatorNotes: Not one person but a voice for peoples conquered by white colonisers: Native Americans and Africans. Hughes uses “I” for a people, as he does elsewhere in the book. The repeated “But the white men came” makes the same history happen to both.
evidence:
I was a red man one time,
But the white men came.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say he lost his “trees” and his “silver moons” rather than his land or his freedom?
facilitatorNotes: The concrete words make the loss personal and sensory: not property but a whole way of living close to forests and night skies. Readers may also notice that the poem’s picture of “jungles” draws on the period’s images of Africa, which Hughes both uses and mourns.
evidence:
I lost my trees.
I lost my silver moons.

questions.prompt: What does “the circus of civilization” say about how conquered peoples were treated, and about civilization itself?
facilitatorNotes: Caged and displayed like circus animals, they become entertainment for others, perhaps recalling real exhibitions of people at fairs. Calling civilization a circus mocks its claim to be superior. “Herd with the many” suggests losing one’s identity in a crowd. Readers can decide whether the ending is bitter, sorrowful or both.
evidence:
Now they’ve caged me
In the circus of civilization.

readings.title: Song for a Banjo Dance
readings.challenge: Hear two voices in one song: the caller of the dance and the music underneath.
readings.focus: A dance call that keeps returning to the setting sun.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. A banjo dance is a lively dance to banjo music. The poem uses Black American speech of the time: “chile” for child, “wil’” for wild, “no mo’” for no more. A “low-down step” is an earthy dance move.

excerpt.locator: “Song for a Banjo Dance,” the whole poem; opens “Shake your brown feet, honey, Shake your brown feet, chile, Shake your brown feet, honey,…”; closes “…(The banjo’s sobbing low) The sun’s going down this very night— Might never rise no mo’.”.

questions.prompt: Most lines tell the dancer what to do. Which lines do something else? What do the lines in brackets add?
facilitatorNotes: The bracketed lines describe the music, which is “sobbing low” and “soft and wil’.” Under the cheerful dance calls the banjo sounds sad. The brackets work like stage directions, giving the mood the speaker does not say out loud.
evidence: (The banjo’s sobbing low)
(The music’s soft and wil’)

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker urge the dancer on because the sun “might never rise no mo’”? Is that a happy thought or a sad one?
facilitatorNotes: It can be read as “live now, while you can”: life is uncertain, so dance. It can also be darker, a fear that something may end tonight, which the sobbing banjo supports. The poem holds both at once, as much blues music does.
evidence: Might never rise no mo’.
So dance with swift feet, honey,

questions.prompt: The dancer gets a name, Liza, only in the last stanza, and the poem ends on the sunset line, not on “Shake ’em.” Why end this way?
facilitatorNotes: Naming her makes the call personal. The first stanza ends on the dance; the last ends on the warning. By the close the darker voice has the final word, so the mood has shifted from play toward lament. Some readers will still hear the dance going on beyond the last line.
evidence: Shake your brown feet, Liza,
Shake ’em, honey chile.

readings.title: Blues Fantasy
readings.challenge: Sort out the different voices in a poem built like a performance.
readings.focus: A blues song of loss that ends in laughter.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. The blues is a Black American form of music, often about loss and trouble, built on repeated lines. Minor melodies sound sad. A trunk is a large travelling case.

excerpt.locator: “Blues Fantasy,” the whole poem; opens “Hey! Hey! That’s what the Blues singers say. Singing minor melodies They laugh, Hey! Hey!”; closes “Laughing, Hey!...Hey! Laugh a loud, Hey! Hey!”.

questions.prompt: “Singing minor melodies / They laugh.” How can blues singers sing sad songs and laugh? Where does the poem itself turn from trouble toward hope?
facilitatorNotes: The blues names pain in order to survive it; singing about trouble is a way of standing up to it. The turn comes in the short stanza “Sun’s gonna shine / Somewhere / Again,” and grows with the railroad ticket. The laughter is not denial; it comes through the sadness.
evidence: Singing minor melodies They laugh,
Sun’s gonna shine Somewhere Again.

questions.prompt: Who is speaking? Find at least three different voices in the poem.
facilitatorNotes: A narrator who explains what “the Blues singers say”; a singer whose man has left her; and someone in the audience calling “Sing ’em, sister!” The poem reads like a live performance, with the crowd taking part.
evidence: That’s what the Blues singers say.
My man’s done left me,
Sing ’em, sister!

questions.prompt: What does the railroad ticket stand for? Does the ending convince you the blues have been cast aside?
facilitatorNotes: The train means leaving: a fresh start somewhere else, and in these years many Black Americans did take the train north to new lives. The poem ends laughing loud. Readers may believe the cure, or suspect the laughter is the blues’ own defiance, since the trouble has not been solved, only answered.
evidence: And when I get on the train I’ll cast my blues aside.
Laugh a loud,

readings.title: When Sue Wears Red
readings.challenge: Follow how a love poem borrows the language of history and of church worship.
readings.focus: A young man watching Susanna Jones in a red dress.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. A cameo is a small portrait carved in stone or shell. The queens of ancient Egypt ruled thousands of years ago. The calls to Jesus echo the shouts of a lively church service.

excerpt.locator: “When Sue Wears Red,” the whole poem; opens “When Susanna Jones wears red Her face is like an ancient cameo Turned brown by the ages.”; closes “Sweet silver trumpets, Jesus!”.

questions.prompt: What two comparisons does the speaker use for Susanna Jones in red? What do they have in common?
facilitatorNotes: Her face is like an ancient cameo “turned brown by the ages,” and she is like an Egyptian queen walking again. Both make her timeless and royal, and both connect her beauty to an African past. Her brown skin is described as something precious, not something to apologise for.
evidence: Her face is like an ancient cameo Turned brown by the ages.
A queen from some time-dead Egyptian night Walks once again.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of the short lines calling on Jesus and trumpets between the descriptions?
facilitatorNotes: They sound like shouts in church, as if her beauty were a kind of glory worth announcing. They grow from a “blast” to “Sweet silver trumpets,” as the speaker’s feeling deepens. Some readers may find mixing worship and romance daring, others joyful; the poem treats delight as something holy.
evidence: Come with a blast of trumpets, Jesus!
Sweet silver trumpets, Jesus!

questions.prompt: The poem ends with “a love-fire sharp like pain.” Why might beauty hurt?
facilitatorNotes: Strong love can feel like pain, especially if it is not returned or cannot be spoken. The poem moves from public images (face, queen) to the speaker’s own heart. Readers can decide whether the pain is longing, awe, or both.
evidence: Burns in my heart a love-fire sharp like pain.

readings.title: Pierrot
readings.challenge: Compare two ways of living set side by side, stanza by stanza.
readings.focus: Steady Simple John and restless Pierrot.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. Pierrot is a figure from old French and Italian comedy: a dreamy, moonstruck clown in white. Pierrette is his sweetheart. A burgher is a respectable townsman.
readings.contentNote: Pierrot leaves his sweetheart and runs away with a married woman.

excerpt.locator: “Pierrot,” the whole poem; opens “I work all day, Said Simple John, Myself a house to buy. I work all day, Said Simple…”; closes “…the moon, And Pierrot ran down the long white road With the burgher’s wife one June.”.

questions.prompt: How is the poem built? Compare the stanzas Simple John speaks with the stanzas about Pierrot.
facilitatorNotes: They alternate. John states his virtues: he works, he is faithful, he is good. Each Pierrot stanza answers with what Pierrot loves: the road, the moon, the stars, all girls, a guitar. One life is settled and dutiful; the other free and wandering.
evidence: I work all day, Said Simple John,
For Pierrot loved the long white road,

questions.prompt: Whose side is the poem on? Look at the name “Simple John” and at the images each man gets.
facilitatorNotes: “Simple” can mean honest or dull. Pierrot gets the lovely images, the moon and “the breath of a rose in June,” so the poem feels the pull of his freedom. But it does not hide the cost: he leaves Pierrette and runs off with another man’s wife. Readers can argue that the poem admires Pierrot, pities him, or warns against him.
evidence: Said Simple John,
But Pierrot left Pierrette.
And the breath of a rose in June.

questions.prompt: The last stanza repeats words from the second with changes. What changes, and why does it matter?
facilitatorNotes: Pierrot once “loved the long white road”; now he “ran down” it. June was the month of roses; now it is the month of running off with the burgher’s wife. His dreams have become actions with consequences for other people.
evidence: And Pierrot loved the moon,
And Pierrot ran down the long white road With the burgher’s wife one June.

readings.title: Young Sailor
readings.challenge: Decide whether a poem admires the life it describes, using its first and last words.
readings.focus: A young sailor who lives only for today.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. The poem comes from a section of the book about the sea and port towns. “Hereafter” means the future, and also life after death.
readings.contentNote: The sailor says money is for spending, wine for drinking and women for loving.

excerpt.locator: “Young Sailor,” the whole poem; opens “He carries His own strength And his own laughter, His own today And his own hereafter,—…”; closes “…And the green sea For strength, And the brown land For laughter. And nothing hereafter.”.

questions.prompt: The first stanza says he carries “his own” strength, laughter, today and hereafter. What does “his own” suggest about him?
facilitatorNotes: He depends on no one and owes nothing: his strength and his future belong to him alone. The repetition stresses independence. Readers may also hear loneliness in it.
evidence: He carries His own strength And his own laughter,

questions.prompt: The second stanza is a set of questions and answers. Who seems to ask, and what pattern do the answers make?
facilitatorNotes: A cautious voice, perhaps the speaker or the world, asks what things are for; the sailor answers at once, and every answer is about using things up: spend, drink, love, joy. Today and tomorrow get the same answer, “For joy,” so there is no saving and no plan.
evidence: What is money for? To spend, he says.
And tomorrow? For joy.

questions.prompt: The poem begins with “his own hereafter” and ends with “nothing hereafter.” Is that a contradiction? Does the poem admire the sailor or warn about him?
facilitatorNotes: He owns his future by refusing to believe in one, and he expects nothing after death. The ending can sound like freedom or like emptiness. Strength and laughter come from “the green sea” and “the brown land,” which suggests admiration, but the last line is bare. Both readings can be argued.
evidence: His own today And his own hereafter,—
And nothing hereafter.

readings.title: Summer Night
readings.challenge: Notice how a poem builds silence, then fills it with feeling that has no clear name.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. A player-piano plays by itself from a punched paper roll; a victrola is a wind-up record player. The court-yard is the space between city buildings.

excerpt.locator: “Summer Night,” the whole poem; opens “The sounds Of the Harlem night Drop one by one into stillness. The last player-piano is…”; closes “…Until the new dawn, Wan and pale, Descends like a white mist Into the court-yard.”.

questions.prompt: Which sounds stop, one by one, at the start? How does the poem make the night grow quiet?
facilitatorNotes: The player-piano, the victrola playing “Jazz Boy Blues,” and finally the crying baby. The repeated “The last…” drops each sound away until the night is “Still as a whispering heartbeat.” Then only the speaker is awake.
evidence: The last player-piano is closed.
The last crying baby sleeps
Still as a whispering heartbeat.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker describe what he feels? Why might he not be able to say what he needs?
facilitatorNotes: He is “Weary as the tired night,” his soul “Empty as the silence,” with “Aching emptiness.” He needs “someone, / Something,” but cannot name it. The vagueness is the point: loneliness or restlessness that has no clear cause. Readers may connect it to love, to youth, or to a search for purpose.
evidence: Empty with a vague, Aching emptiness,
Needing someone, Something.

questions.prompt: Dawn usually means hope. Is this dawn hopeful?
facilitatorNotes: It is “Wan and pale” and comes down “like a white mist”: weak, cold, blurry. The night ends, but nothing suggests the emptiness has. Some readers will still see relief in morning arriving at all.
evidence: Until the new dawn, Wan and pale, Descends like a white mist Into the court-yard.

readings.title: The White Ones
readings.challenge: Explain how a very short poem gets its force from what it refuses to say.
readings.focus: A speaker who will not hate those who hurt him.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. When this book appeared in 1926, Black Americans faced segregation and racist violence across the United States.
readings.contentNote: The poem calls the treatment of Black Americans by white people “torture.”

excerpt.locator: “The White Ones,” the whole poem; opens “I do not hate you, For your faces are beautiful, too. I do not hate you, Your faces are…”; closes “…splendor, too. Yet why do you torture me, O, white strong ones, Why do you torture me?”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker grant to “the white ones”? Why does the small word “too” matter?
facilitatorNotes: He grants that their faces are beautiful, “whirling lights of loveliness and splendor.” “Too” quietly claims the same beauty for himself and his people: he is speaking as an equal. It turns a compliment into a claim of equal worth.
evidence: For your faces are beautiful, too.
Your faces are whirling lights of loveliness and splendor, too.

questions.prompt: The poem ends with a question asked twice. Why ask, rather than accuse?
facilitatorNotes: A question demands an answer and puts the burden on “the white ones” to explain what cannot be justified. “Strong” points to who holds power. Repeating it makes the plea harder to ignore.
evidence: Yet why do you torture me, O, white strong ones,
Why do you torture me?

questions.prompt: Is refusing to hate a strength or a weakness here? Use the poem’s restraint in your answer.
facilitatorNotes: The calm “I do not hate you” makes the word “torture” land harder. The speaker keeps his dignity and his moral ground. Readers may argue that anger would be just as justified; the poem’s power comes from choosing not to show it, and that choice can be discussed rather than taken for granted.
evidence: I do not hate you,

readings.title: Poem (“The night is beautiful”)
readings.challenge: Find the pattern in a very short poem, and notice where it breaks.
readings.focus: Three beautiful things in the sky, and three beautiful things about “my people.”
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. In the 1920s, advertisements, cartoons and films often mocked Black faces and features.

excerpt.locator: “Poem,” the one that begins “The night is beautiful,” the whole poem; opens “The night is beautiful, So the faces of my people.”; closes “Beautiful, also, is the sun. Beautiful, also, are the souls of my people.”.

questions.prompt: The poem pairs three things in the sky with three things about “my people.” Match them up. What links each pair?
facilitatorNotes: Night with faces, stars with eyes, sun with souls. Darkness, light shining out of darkness, and warmth and life. The pairs move inward, from faces to eyes to souls.
evidence: The stars are beautiful, So the eyes of my people.

questions.prompt: Why might comparing faces to the night be a bold choice in 1926?
facilitatorNotes: Poems and prejudice often treated darkness as bad or ugly. Hughes makes it beautiful and claims that beauty for Black faces. He states it calmly as a fact, not an argument.
evidence: The night is beautiful, So the faces of my people.

questions.prompt: What changes in the last stanza, and why might the souls come last?
facilitatorNotes: The sky moves from night to day, and “Beautiful” jumps to the front of the line, with “also” added. The sun is the largest light, and it goes with the souls: the poem ends with beauty that is not about appearance at all.
evidence: Beautiful, also, is the sun. Beautiful, also, are the souls of my people.

readings.title: A Black Pierrot
readings.challenge: Follow a heartbreak through one night, and decide how serious it is.
readings.focus: A clown in love is turned down, weeps till dawn, and goes out again.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. Pierrot is the sad clown of old French pantomime, dressed in white with a whitened face, who loves and loses. Gay-colored here means brightly coloured.

excerpt.locator: “A Black Pierrot,” the whole poem; opens “I am a black Pierrot: She did not love me, So I crept away into the night And the night…”; closes “…like a balloon without air, I went forth in the morning To seek a new brown love.”.

questions.prompt: What does the Pierrot do in each stanza after “She did not love me”? How does time move through the poem?
facilitatorNotes: He creeps away into the night, weeps until dawn, and goes out in the morning to seek a new love. One night carries him from hiding, to grief, to starting again.
evidence: So I crept away into the night And the night was black, too.
I went forth in the morning To seek a new brown love.

questions.prompt: Why might Hughes make his Pierrot black? What does the word “too” do in the first two stanzas?
facilitatorNotes: The traditional Pierrot has a white face; Hughes claims the famous sad clown for a Black speaker. “Too” makes the world match his feelings: the night is black like him, and the dawn bleeds as his heart does.
evidence: I am a black Pierrot:
Dripped blood over the eastern hills And my heart was bleeding, too.

questions.prompt: Look at the balloon and the last line. Is this heartbreak tragic, funny or hopeful?
facilitatorNotes: A soul “shrunken like a balloon without air” is a sad image and also a comic one, right for a clown. Then he simply goes looking for “a new brown love.” Readers may see resilience, fickleness or brave pretending.
evidence: So with my once gay-colored soul Shrunken like a balloon without air,

readings.title: Poem: To the Black Beloved
readings.challenge: Follow a love poem built from denials, and work out what each denial is really saying.
readings.focus: A lover tells his beloved she is not beautiful, and then says something greater.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. “Thou art” and “thou hast” are old forms of “you are” and “you have,” used in prayers and in love poetry. An altar of jewels is a richly decorated church altar; luminous means giving off light. “Nightness” is an unusual word built like “darkness.”

excerpt.locator: “Poem,” subtitled “To the Black Beloved,” the whole poem; opens “To the Black Beloved”; closes “…jewels, Would pale in the light Of thy darkness, Pale in the light Of thy nightness.”.

questions.prompt: Each stanza says “Thou art not” and then “Yet thou hast.” What does the beloved lack, and what does she have instead?
facilitatorNotes: Not beautiful, but a loveliness surpassing beauty; not good, but a purity surpassing goodness; not luminous, but a darkness that outshines jewels. Each time, the missing quality is replaced by something greater.
evidence: Thou art not beautiful Yet thou hast A loveliness Surpassing beauty.
Thou art not good Yet thou hast A purity Surpassing goodness.

questions.prompt: Why might the speaker begin by denying that she is beautiful? Whose idea of beauty might he be answering?
facilitatorNotes: He seems to answer a world whose standard of “beautiful” left out Black women. He lets the word go and claims something better. Some readers will hear a lover’s honesty instead; either way, the denial makes the praise stronger.
evidence: Ah, My black one,

questions.prompt: What is surprising about “the light / Of thy darkness”? Why might the last stanza be the longest?
facilitatorNotes: Darkness gives off light, enough to make a jewelled altar pale. The poem reverses the usual idea that light is good and dark is bad. The final stanza grows longer as the praise builds and ends on a new word, “nightness.”
evidence: Would pale in the light Of thy darkness, Pale in the light Of thy nightness.

readings.title: Joy
readings.challenge: Enjoy a poem that sets up a grand search and ends with a surprise.
readings.focus: A poet goes looking for Joy and finds her somewhere he did not expect.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. In old poems a nymph is a lovely nature spirit, often chased by gods and poets. A butcher’s cart delivered meat from the shop. Gay here means merry.

excerpt.locator: “Joy,” the whole poem; opens “I went to look for Joy, Slim, dancing Joy, Gay, laughing Joy, Bright-eyed Joy,— And I…”; closes “…the arms of the butcher boy! Such company, such company, As keeps this young nymph, Joy!”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker picture Joy before he finds her? What kind of search does he seem to expect?
facilitatorNotes: Joy is a girl: slim, dancing, laughing, bright-eyed. He sets out as if on a poetic quest for something rare and lovely.
evidence: Slim, dancing Joy, Gay, laughing Joy, Bright-eyed Joy,—

questions.prompt: Where does he find her? Why is that surprising?
facilitatorNotes: Driving the butcher’s cart in the arms of the butcher boy: plain work and ordinary young love, not a poetic setting. The grand search ends in a joke.
evidence: Driving the butcher’s cart In the arms of the butcher boy!

questions.prompt: “Such company, such company” — is the speaker shocked, amused or a little jealous? What is the poem saying about where happiness is found?
facilitatorNotes: The tone is mock-scandalised, and perhaps rueful: Joy is with someone else. Happiness is found in everyday people and work, not where poets look for it. Readers can disagree about the tone.
evidence: Such company, such company, As keeps this young nymph, Joy!

readings.title: A Farewell
readings.challenge: Hear what a short goodbye says and what it leaves unsaid.
readings.focus: A young man leaves respectable people for a wandering life.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. Hughes worked as a sailor on voyages to Africa and Europe as a young man. Gypsies here means wandering people who travel from place to place; pious folk are devout, churchgoing people.

excerpt.locator: “A Farewell,” the whole poem; opens “With gypsies and sailors, Wanderers of the hills and seas, I go to seek my fortune. With…”; closes “…But you will not miss me,— You who live between the hills And have never seen the seas.”.

questions.prompt: Whom does the speaker go with, and whom does he leave?
facilitatorNotes: He goes with gypsies and sailors, “wanderers of the hills and seas,” to seek his fortune, and parts from “pious folk and fair.” Two ways of life: wandering and settled respectability.
evidence: With gypsies and sailors, Wanderers of the hills and seas, I go to seek my fortune.
With pious folk and fair I must have a parting.

questions.prompt: “But you will not miss me” — is the speaker hurt, defiant or relieved?
facilitatorNotes: The dash before it suggests a pause. He seems sure the people he leaves never valued him; the line can be read as hurt, proud or simply honest. Readers should say which words support their reading.
evidence: But you will not miss me,—

questions.prompt: Why does it matter that the people he leaves “have never seen the seas”?
facilitatorNotes: They live “between the hills,” closed in, and cannot understand what he goes looking for. The sea stands for freedom and the wide world. The line may carry a little pity as well as a little pride.
evidence: You who live between the hills And have never seen the seas.

readings.title: Poem (“We have tomorrow”)
readings.challenge: See how a nine-line poem turns time into pictures.
readings.focus: Tomorrow, yesterday and today, each given its own image.
readings.context: Langston Hughes (1902–1967) published The Weary Blues, his first book of poems, in 1926, when he was a young poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the flowering of Black writing, music and art centred in Harlem, New York. Hughes often made new compound words by joining two words with a hyphen.

excerpt.locator: “Poem,” the one that begins “We have tomorrow,” the whole poem; opens “We have tomorrow Bright before us Like a flame.”; closes “And dawn-today Broad arch above the road we came.”.

questions.prompt: What picture does the poem give for tomorrow, for yesterday and for today?
facilitatorNotes: Tomorrow is a bright flame ahead; yesterday is a “night-gone thing, a sun-down name”; today is dawn and a broad arch. The past is dark and finished, and the present and future are light.
evidence: Bright before us Like a flame.
A night-gone thing, A sun-down name.

questions.prompt: Who might “we” be? What does “the road we came” suggest about the past?
facilitatorNotes: In a book about Black life in America, “we” can be Black Americans, the young, or anyone reading. A road suggests a long, hard journey that is now behind them.
evidence: We have tomorrow
the road we came

questions.prompt: Why “dawn-today” and an “arch”? What feeling does the poem leave you with?
facilitatorNotes: Today is a beginning, and the arch is like a gateway or a rainbow over the road already travelled. The compound words make time into images. The feeling is hope that remembers the hard road without being ruled by it.
evidence: And dawn-today Broad arch above
